title: Mobile sign permits extended from 30 days to a full year (By-law 2066)
summary: After businesses complained when enforcement of the 2015 zoning by-law began, council amended the mobile sign rules so a business can get an annual (365-day) permit instead of 30-day permits with 30-day gaps and a 90-day yearly cap. Councillors Siemens and a Councillor Penner opposed first reading, arguing it makes temporary signs permanent and ignores the earlier public consultation on the city's appearance.
status_detail: First reading carried Dec 15, 2015 with Siemens and one Councillor Penner speaking against; second and third reading carried Jan 19, 2016 (no objections at the public hearing) and took effect immediately. Council kept the 365-day permit when it revisited the rules in Sept 2016.
figures: Old rule: 30-day permits, 30 days down between permits, 90 days a year maximum; new rule: one annual permit (transcript 2016-01-19 0:09:25). Comparison cited: Morden and Selkirk no time limit, Winkler 12 months (Zwaagstra, 2015-12-15 0:20:49); Portage, Brandon, Niverville stricter (Councillor Penner, 0:17:29).
reasons: businesses-support-it: Businesses should be able to advertise on their own property; there were no complaints before enforcement began. (Michael Zwaagstra); protect-residents: Against: a year-long permit is a permanent sign; signs will deteriorate. (Jac Siemens); study-first: Against: the wider public was not consulted; only sign users were heard. (Councillor Penner (Susan or Cari Penner; not identified))
public: Business owners using mobile signs had complained in fall 2015 (as reported by council); no objections were registered at the Jan 19, 2016 public hearing.
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (first and second reading); Earl Funk (third reading)
seconder: John Fehr (first, as heard 'Councillor Faris'); Earl Funk (second); Michael Zwaagstra (third)
vote: First reading carried with opposition (Siemens and one Councillor Penner spoke against); second and third reading carried, opponents not named
notes: Who opposed second/third reading on Jan 19, 2016 is not stated in the transcript ('Opposed? Carried').

title: Ground-floor commercial requirement waived for housing projects near downtown
summary: Council let developers build housing in commercial zones near downtown without the required ground-floor commercial space: three-storey apartments on Hanover Street in a C-1 zone (Feb 2016), and at 486 Main Street (C-2, central business district) a phased project with residential first and the commercial building required in phase 2 by development agreement (Sept 2017). A councillor said an earlier Main Street exception had never produced its promised commercial space.
status_detail: Both approved; 486 Main Street commercial component tied to phase 2 in the development agreement (follow-through not verified).
reasons: market-decides: Mixed use still achieved; developer cited empty commercial units. (Michael Zwaagstra); study-first: Asked how the city would enforce commercial space promised later. (Susan Penner)
public: Developer C.B. (Hanover Street) said residential fits better and brings people downtown; at 486 Main, developer said many commercial units in Steinbach were empty; neighbours raised privacy and drainage.
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (486 Main conditional use); John Fehr (variance)

title: Sign variances and electronic-sign approvals granted to Main Street businesses
summary: Council routinely approved business sign requests along Main Street in 2016–2017: an electronic message board at 236 Main (Feb 2016), a 30-foot, 120 sq ft pylon at 180 Main where 20 feet is the limit (Jul 2016), third-party advertising on an existing electronic sign (Aug 2016), and sign approvals at 850 Main for Synex Manufacturing (Sep 2016, Aug 2017).
status_detail: All recorded requests approved ('Carried'); no denials of business sign variances found in the period.
figures: 180 Main Street: 30 ft height vs 20 ft allowed in C-2 (transcript 2016-07-19).
reasons: businesses-support-it: Sign will enhance the business's chance of success; precedent exists down the street. (Councillor Penner (Susan or Cari Penner; not identified))

title: Retail, a hotel and a church allowed on light-industrial land by conditional use
summary: Council approved conditional uses putting non-industrial uses on M-1 light-industrial land: Menno Mart, a charity resale store at 62 Life Science Parkway (Feb 2016); a hotel at 375 North Front Drive on PTH 52 West, which the applicant said would create 30–35 jobs (Sep 2016); and a place of worship at 88 Acres Drive (June 2017).
status_detail: All three approved; no objections recorded.
figures: Hotel: 30–35 new jobs claimed by the applicant (2016-09-06 0:16:34).
reasons: businesses-support-it: Visitors to the 2016 Summer Games had to stay and spend in other towns. (John Fehr); businesses-support-it: Someone wants to invest in the city. (Chris Goertzen)
public: Applicants (initials only): B.S. for Menno Mart; H.B. for the hotel; A.A. for the church.
mover: Jac Siemens (Menno Mart); John Fehr (hotel, church)

title: Chamber of Commerce asks for a joint council–Chamber committee to rewrite the mobile sign rules
summary: The Steinbach Chamber of Commerce (vice-president T.S.) thanked council for the quick fix on permit length but said sign sizes, large shopping centres and non-profit signs were still a problem, and formally asked for an ad hoc committee of three councillors, three Chamber representatives and staff to write an entirely new mobile sign by-law. The mayor promised a quick response but no specific committee.
status_detail: No ad hoc committee was struck (none recorded); the issues were worked through at committee of the whole with written Chamber submissions and administration, and council rewrote the rules in Sept–Nov 2016 (see 2016-mobile-sign-rewrite). The mayor thanked the Chamber for its input when the by-law passed.
reasons: businesses-support-it: Wants a balanced approach that respects businesses, community groups and the city's appearance; promised not to drag it out. (Chris Goertzen)
public: T.S. (Chamber vice-president) asked for a joint committee; Chamber cited sign sizes, large properties and limits on non-profit signs.
notes: The Sept 6, 2016 discussion says the draft followed 'additional submissions that were provided by members of the business community as well as the Steinbach Chamber of Commerce'.

title: 0.5% business tax levied each year and passed to the Chamber of Commerce
summary: Council passed the annual business tax levy by-law (By-law 2063 in 2016; the 2017 by-law in March 2017) continuing a 0.5% business tax. The money is collected by the city and turned over to the Chamber of Commerce for its operations, less 5% for collection. The Chamber's yearly grant request letters (Dec 2016, Dec 2017) were taken as information and handled in the budget.
status_detail: 2016 by-law: first and second reading Apr 5, third reading May 3, 2016; 2017 by-law first and second reading Mar 21, 2017. City manager described the Chamber arrangement as ongoing.
figures: 0.5% business tax levy (2016-04-05_part2 0:35:07); city keeps 5% for collection (2016-12-06 0:17:09). Dollar amount not stated in the transcripts.
reasons: partner-money: Business tax is collected and passed through to the Chamber ('in and out'). (John Fehr)
public: Steinbach Chamber of Commerce grant request letters and annual financial statements (Dec 6, 2016; Dec 19, 2017).
mover: Councillor Penner (2016 first reading; not identified); Zwaagstra (2016 third reading)

title: Downtown land assembly continues: five houses bought near the arenas and Hanover Street
summary: Continuing a roughly 20-year strategy, council bought residential lots around the T.G. Smith Centre and arenas for future recreation, a performing arts centre or parking: 376 Hanover St (Apr 2016), 385 Elmdale St (Sep 2016, completing the Elmdale frontage), 316 Hanover St (Oct 2016), 326 Hanover St (Nov 2016) and 316 Barkman Ave (May 2017). Houses are rented until needed. Siemens voted against the first, saying the city was taking starter homes off the market without a plan.
status_detail: All five purchases carried; Siemens opposed the Apr 5, 2016 purchase. Administration estimated the city's vacant downtown lots could hold about 400 parking stalls (Apr 5, 2016). No development plan for the assembled land was adopted in this period.
figures: 376 Hanover $205,000 (2016-04-05_part2 0:27:30); 326 Hanover $331,200 (2016-11-01 0:05:36); 316 Barkman $150,000 (2017-05-16 0:18:47); ~400 stalls possible (2016-04-05_part2 0:54:55). Funded from general operating fund and reserves.
reasons: study-first: Against: removes starter homes; no plan in place for the land. (Jac Siemens); businesses-support-it: Long-term strategy so land is available for recreation or parking as the city grows. (Michael Zwaagstra)
mover: Councillor Penner (376 Hanover, 316 Hanover, 316 Barkman; not identified); Michael Zwaagstra (385 Elmdale, 326 Hanover)
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra; Earl Funk; Councillor Penner; Jac Siemens (316 Barkman)
vote: all carried; 376 Hanover with Siemens against

title: Industrial condominium subdivisions approved (16 lots on Park Road West; 8 bays on Industrial Road)
summary: Council approved privately developed industrial bare-land condominiums: 16 light-industrial lots on the old campground at 236 Park Road West (Apr 5, 2016) and an 8-bay industrial condominium at 131 Industrial Road (Aug 1, 2017). Councillor Siemens noted small bays can act as incubators for small businesses.
status_detail: Both approved subject to development agreements.
reasons: businesses-support-it: Small rental bays are a starting point for growing businesses. (Jac Siemens)

title: Private commercial park on PTH 12 North allowed lower road standard (swale drainage, no curb and gutter)
summary: Steinbach Land Holding / Northview Developments, building a private C-3 commercial-industrial subdivision on PTH 12 North (Petro-Canada card lock committed), asked to use open swale drainage without curb and gutter instead of the city's urban standard. Administration warned it was a citywide spec change and unfair to other C-3 owners. Deferred Apr 5 for a report; approved May 3, 2016 as a one-time exception through the development agreement.
status_detail: Approved May 3, 2016 (gravity sewer, piped water, 32-ft concrete street, swale drainage, no curb and gutter). Mayor Goertzen declared a perceived conflict and left; Deputy Mayor Fehr chaired.
figures: 32-ft concrete streets vs 24-ft at Hespeler; standard spec manual about 150 pages (transcript 2016-05-03).
reasons: businesses-support-it: Private developer building at its own cost; no major manufacturer in 10 years; industrial parks sit empty. (Jac Siemens); cost: Need very affordable places for businesses to locate; relax specs. (Cari Penner); fairness-precedent: Against: it changes the spec for all C-3 land and sets a precedent; need a level playing field. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Developer representatives D.C. and B.S. said strict specs and delays cost jobs and that 'one size doesn't fit all'.
vote: carried; Zwaagstra stated he would vote against; tally not recorded; mayor absent (conflict)
notes: Diarization mixes labels in both meetings; quotes chosen only where the chair names the speaker immediately before.

title: Eastman Tourism asks the city to join the regional tourism association
summary: Eastman Tourism, one of six provincially funded regional tourism associations, said Steinbach had never been a member and asked the city to join for $1,500 a year and name a tourism contact, offering joint marketing and help with the 2016 Manitoba Summer Games. Council asked questions and took it as information.
status_detail: No motion; no later decision on membership found in the 2016–2017 transcripts.
figures: Membership $1,500 per year, prorated (2016-06-21 0:21:37); 15 of 24 RMs and towns are members (0:12:55).
public: L.G. (volunteer, community economic development officer for the RM of Ritchot) and J.D. (executive director) presented for Eastman Tourism.

title: Mobile sign rules rewritten to match existing practice (By-law 2065)
summary: Working through administration's options clause by clause, council mostly chose the least restrictive option: standard 9x10-foot signs for non-profit campaigns and in downtown C-1/C-2 zones, 365-day permits kept, mobile signs not counted against a site's sign allowance, and mobile signs allowed on lots with electronic message boards. At the Oct 18 hearing the Chamber showed setbacks would push signs into parking lots, so council cut the front setback to 1 foot for all signs; it referred lit/digital mobile signs back to administration. Adopted Nov 1, 2016.
status_detail: Second and third reading carried Nov 1, 2016. Management's recommendations to return to 90-day permits and to count mobile signs in the site sign allowance were rejected. Digital mobile signs remain not allowed, left to the next zoning by-law review.
figures: Non-profit campaign signs: option 2 (56 sq ft) defeated, option 3 (standard ~85 sq ft / 9x10 ft) carried; front setback 1 ft, side 2 ft for all mobile signs (transcripts 2016-09-06, 2016-10-18 0:42:38); max 1 mobile sign per use, 2 per lot.
reasons: businesses-support-it: Rules should let existing advertising continue; cutting signs in half downtown is not business-friendly. (Michael Zwaagstra); businesses-support-it: The spirit of the sign by-law is to allow advertising; business people will limit themselves. (Earl Funk); protect-residents: Against 365-day permits: a year-long sign is a permanent sign. (Jac Siemens); protect-residents: Against mobile signs beside electronic boards: clutter; development agreements already promised no extra signs. (Chris Goertzen); study-first: Digital signs should be addressed now; then agreed to defer to the zoning review. (John Fehr)
public: Chamber representatives T.S. and G.B. presented examples (Shoppers Drug Mart, Quality Details, Good and Natural) where a 10-ft setback would put signs in parking-lot driving aisles; P.R. (Synex Manufacturing) asked that digital mobile signs be allowed; N.P. (Penner Signs) said there is effectively only one standard mobile sign size.
vote: Second and third reading carried; several clause votes divided on Sept 6, 2016 (see split_votes)
notes: Clause votes on Sept 6 are recorded only as 'Carried'/'defeated' with some members stating their votes; full tallies not given.

title: Mobile signs kept out of the public right-of-way; Great Canadian Oil Change request declined
summary: On Sept 6, 2016 council kept the ban on mobile signs in the public right-of-way (Fehr against, citing the Pistons' game-day signs). When Great Canadian Oil Change wrote in November asking to place a mobile sign in the right-of-way, council took the letter as information by consensus, so the rule stood.
status_detail: Request declined by consensus Nov 15, 2016; administration to reply to the business.
reasons: protect-residents: Right-of-way is for safe travel; signs there cause visibility and safety problems. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Great Canadian Oil Change (letter) asked to place a mobile sign in the right-of-way.
vote: Sept 6: carried, Fehr against; Nov 15: consensus to take as information

title: Councillor Susan Penner: regional business draw does not mean a regional tax base
summary: In her opening remarks, Susan Penner said Steinbach's regional shopping and business draw creates a false impression of its resources: new business taxes go to servicing growth, and Steinbach taxpayers carry regional facilities. She asked whether surrounding RMs could partner on regional facilities.
status_detail: A statement, not a motion. Regional cost-sharing was not acted on in this period.
figures: Population about 15,000; serves a region of 30,000–60,000 (2016-09-20 0:00:01).
reasons: cost: Growth costs money; new business property taxes cover infrastructure for new properties. (Susan Penner)

title: Non-residential capital development fees raised 2.5% (By-law 2071)
summary: Council raised residential and non-residential capital development fees by 2.5%, about inflation, to pay for growth-related infrastructure such as sidewalks.
status_detail: Second and third reading carried Nov 1, 2016.
reasons: cost: Growth has an impact on the city; keep fees near inflation so they are not too high. (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Request to allow digital (lit) mobile signs deferred to a future zoning review
summary: Synex Manufacturing, a local sign maker, said the by-law's ban on illuminated mobile signs shuts out its rentable digital display trailers. Council referred the question back to administration on Oct 18, 2016, then on Nov 1 adopted the sign rules without allowing digital mobile signs, agreeing to look at it in the zoning review that would follow annexation.
status_detail: Not allowed as of Nov 2016; administration said the next zoning review could be 18–24 months after the annexation review. No later decision found in 2016–2017.
figures: Administration: about three digital mobile signs in Manitoba (Winnipeg, Winkler, PTH 52) (transcript 2016-11-01 0:17:48).
reasons: study-first: No local requests yet; comfortable reviewing it in the by-law review. (John Fehr); study-first: Wanted it addressed now rather than in a year or two (Oct 18 referral). (Jac Siemens)
public: P.R. (Synex Manufacturing) asked that digital mobile signs be allowed; a conditional use for each event would not be financially feasible.
vote: referral carried; by-law adopted Nov 1 without the change

title: City buys back and resells industrial lots on Acres Drive and Industrial Road
summary: The city develops and sells its own industrial lots with build-within-a-time-limit agreements. In Feb 2017 it used a buy-back clause to repurchase undeveloped 88 Acres Drive for $49,300 (Zwaagstra against: the city already had unsold industrial lots); it sold 127 Industrial Road at its $75,000 list price in May 2017 and resold 88 Acres Drive for $78,000 in June 2017 to a church group after approving a place of worship there.
status_detail: Buy-back carried Feb 21, 2017; 127 Industrial Road sold May 16, 2017; 88 Acres Drive resold June 6, 2017 (conditional use for a church approved the same night).
reasons: market-decides: Let the owner sell privately; city should not add to its unsold industrial inventory. (Michael Zwaagstra); businesses-support-it: City develops industrial land to recover costs and get buildings built; buy-back at 85% benefits the city. (Chris Goertzen)
mover: Councillor Penner (buy-back; not identified); Michael Zwaagstra (127 Industrial Rd sale); John Fehr spoke for the resale
seconder: John Fehr (buy-back and 127 sale); Michael Zwaagstra (resale)
vote: buy-back carried with Zwaagstra against; sales carried

title: City objects to a commercial-industrial rezoning just outside its border, then forms a joint committee with La Broquerie
summary: When the RM of La Broquerie considered rezoning land just outside Steinbach to rural commercial-industrial without the consultation required in the shared transition zone, council voted to object and send the city manager and planner to the Municipal Board. After public friction in the fall, the mayor met the reeve and the two municipalities agreed to a joint action committee like the one with Hanover.
status_detail: Objection filed (Municipal Board hearing May 2, 2017; outcome not found in the transcripts). Joint action committee created Nov 7, 2017 with Mayor Goertzen and Councillor Fehr.
reasons: protect-residents: Transition zone and duty to consult must be respected. (Michael Zwaagstra); businesses-support-it: Neighbours' growth is the city's growth; cooperate rather than divide. (Chris Goertzen)

title: Main Street intersection bands in the central business district rebuilt, partly (50/50 with the province)
summary: Tenders to replace worn intersection bands across downtown Main Street came in about $160,000 over the $360,000 budget, so council awarded only part of the work (Craker and Friesen plus repairs), cost-shared 50/50 with the province, and hoped to finish later.
status_detail: Partial award to Maple Leaf Construction; remaining intersections deferred to a future year.
reasons: partner-money: Province pays 50% only up to the budget; above it the city would pay 100%. (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: City licenses the Chamber's 'More for You Here' slogan
summary: Council approved a licensing agreement letting the city use the Chamber of Commerce's trademarked 'More for You Here' slogan to promote city facilities and events, rather than run a competing slogan. Fehr was uneasy that the city may not use it to promote business.
status_detail: Agreement approved; to be reviewed in three years.
reasons: partner-money: Chamber did the research; makes sense to benefit from its work. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Agreement drafted by the Steinbach Chamber of Commerce.

title: Paved-parking rule relaxed case by case for businesses on gravel roads
summary: The zoning by-law requires hard-surfaced parking. Council granted variances to Keystone Agri-Motive, an implement dealer (June 2017), and to the Rental House on Park Road West (Dec 2017, after the fact and against administration's recommendation). In Oct 2017 Fehr asked for the rule to be reviewed for businesses on gravel roads, and it was flagged for the zoning review.
status_detail: Variances approved June 20 and Dec 5, 2017 (Dec 5 with Zwaagstra and the mayor against). Policy change referred to the post-annexation zoning review; no change adopted in 2017.
figures: Keystone Agri-Motive would otherwise need 50 paved stalls (Zwaagstra, 2017-06-20 0:29:48).
reasons: cost: Paving next to a gravel road is costly and pointless. (John Fehr); fairness-precedent: Neighbouring dealer had to pave; equity in applying by-laws (June 2017). (Councillor Penner (Susan or Cari Penner; not identified)); fairness-precedent: Against the Dec 2017 variance: development agreement signed, ignorance is not an excuse. (Michael Zwaagstra); fairness-precedent: Against Dec 2017: hold people to development agreements. (Chris Goertzen)
public: Applicant O.K. (Rental House) said customers come from construction and farm sites and the road is gravel.
mover: Jac Siemens (June); Councillor Penner (Dec; not identified)
vote: June: carried; Dec: carried, Zwaagstra and Goertzen against

title: Parking fines raised from $15 to $40, kept low so downtown shoppers are not scared off
summary: With parking tickets moving to municipal adjudication, council raised the general parking fine from $15 to $40 ($20 if paid within 7 days). Zwaagstra said fines should not be so high that people avoid parking downtown and shopping; Fehr wanted $100.
status_detail: Carried July 18, 2017 (R17-140). Minutes record it as unanimous although Fehr said he would not support it.
reasons: businesses-support-it: Too-high fines discourage parking and shopping downtown. (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Council asks Ottawa to drop the 2017 small business tax changes
summary: At the Chamber of Commerce's request, Councillor Susan Penner moved that the city write the federal government asking it to abandon proposed changes to small business corporate taxation (income sprinkling, passive income, succession). Councillors spoke from their own experience as business owners; the motion carried.
status_detail: Motion carried Sept 5, 2017; letter to be sent. Ottawa later scaled back the proposals (federal follow-up not verified from these sources).
figures: Councillor's figures: 98% of Canadian businesses are small, 71% of Canadians employed by small business (2017-09-05 0:43:38).
reasons: businesses-support-it: Low small-business taxes let owners reinvest and hire; Chamber asked for support. (Susan Penner)
public: Steinbach Chamber of Commerce letter asked council to support its letter to the Minister of Finance.
decision_source: transcript; mover named by SteinbachOnline ('Steinbach opposes federal tax changes for small business')
notes: Funk's remarks are split across several diarization labels (L/H/M); not quoted for that reason.

title: Commercial redesignation of 80 Brandt Street refused to protect a residential block
summary: Envision (Association for Community Living) asked to redesignate 80 Brandt Street from residential to commercial to build offices. After residents objected to future commercial creep along the block, council denied the official community plan change, saying the area should be reviewed as a whole in the 2018 plan review.
status_detail: First reading Nov 7, 2017; OCP amendment denied Dec 5, 2017, so the rezoning hearing was not held.
reasons: protect-residents: Long-term change; review the whole area in the 2018 plan review. (Jac Siemens); study-first: Likes the use but cannot control future commercial uses once redesignated. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Residents (e.g., K.L.) opposed commercial creep, traffic and noise; a nearby business owner noted vacant commercial buildings on Main Street.

title: Golf club's $500,000 grant request refused, then 40 acres bought for $500,000 and leased back for $1 a year
summary: The Steinbach Fly-In Golf Club, in financial difficulty, first asked council in closed session for a $500,000 grant, which was refused. Council then agreed to buy 40 acres of the course for $500,000 over three years and lease it back for $1 a year to about 2083. Supporters called it a strategic land investment that keeps a regional attraction open; opponents called it a bailout unfair to other businesses and non-profits that are refused grants, and objected that a motion to hear the club in public was defeated 4-3.
status_detail: Purchase carried 4-3 on Dec 5, 2017; lease carried (Zwaagstra against). Possession Mar 1, 2018.
figures: $500,000 purchase, paid over 3 years from a $300,000/year land budget (Fehr, 2017-12-05 1:01:04); lease $1/yr to about 2083 (0:58:52); club claims ~$2M/yr local economic impact (Siemens, 1:03:07).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Against: a bailout benefiting the club and its lender; unfair to other business owners. (Earl Funk); fairness-precedent: Against: unfair to non-profits that are refused grants (identified by elimination). (Susan Penner); not-council-role: Against: tax dollars to keep a private club operating; no appraisal; no public input. (Michael Zwaagstra); businesses-support-it: For: the course brings visitors and economic activity; Chamber endorsed it. (Cari Penner); cost: For: land worth more than the price; council does not give operating grants but buys land. (John Fehr)
public: Steinbach Chamber of Commerce letter endorsing the club's value to the community (cited by Councillor Cari Penner).
decision_source: transcript; 4-3 count confirmed by SteinbachOnline ('city council agrees to buy 40 acres from the golf course')

title: New community plan and zoning by-law cover nearly 3,000 annexed acres
summary: The 2017 annexation from the RM of Hanover added just under 3,000 acres, less than the city asked for. In 2018 council adopted a new official community plan (By-law 2099) and zoning by-law (By-law 2100) covering the new land, after open houses; the zoning changes included the gravel-road paving exemption and conditional-use retail in light industrial zones.
status_detail: OCP third reading R18-242 and zoning by-law third reading R18-243, both unanimous, Oct 16, 2018.
figures: Just under 3,000 acres annexed (Warkentin 2018-02-06 0:04:58); 2017 permits just under $60 million (same).
public: Residents of the annexed area raised situations at open houses (Fehr 2018-06-05).

title: 2016 Manitoba Summer Games reported $2.3 million of activity in Steinbach
summary: The host society reported an economic impact study done with the Steinbach Chamber of Commerce and Sport Manitoba: over 6,000 participants and spectators, $660,000 in visitor spending and $2.3 million of economic activity in Steinbach. Councillors called the city's support a good investment.
status_detail: Received as information; the host society returned $4,203.45 to the city.
figures: Visitor spending $660,000; total spending $1.9 million; $2.6 million activity in Manitoba incl. $2.3 million in Steinbach; city share of surplus $4,203.45 (presentation 2018-03-06 0:42:11, 0:48:31).
public: Host society representatives (initials not needed) presented.

title: Business tax kept at 0.5% each year, with a matching grant to the Chamber of Commerce
summary: Council passed the business tax levy at 0.5% in 2018, 2019 and 2020. The city manager explained that when the rate fell from 1% about 15 years earlier, council began an annual operating grant to the Steinbach Chamber of Commerce roughly equal to the business tax raised. The Chamber's grant requests (Dec 2018, Nov 2019) were received as information and the grants were paid. In 2020 a councillor said the Chamber uses the money for immigration work and its own operations.
public: Steinbach Chamber of Commerce grant requests received Dec 4, 2018 and Nov 5, 2019; Nov 3, 2020 Chamber letter reported its year, thanked council and asked for continued support (minutes).
mover: Michael Zwaagstra; Michael Zwaagstra; Jac Siemens
seconder: Earl Funk; Susan Penner; Susan Penner
notes: May 19, 2020 minutes not available; 2nd reading (Zwaagstra / a Councillor Penner) and 3rd reading (moved and seconded by the two Councillors Hiebert) of By-law 2151 carried per the transcript (2020-05-19 0:58:34-0:59:09). The 2020 Chamber grant amount is reported after this period.

title: Cannabis retail question placed on the Oct 2018 ballot
summary: Ahead of legalization, an April 2018 opening remark weighed a plebiscite and restrictive zoning for cannabis stores. On July 17, 2018 the mayor added a cannabis plebiscite item to the agenda. On Aug 7 councillors referred to the cannabis question already going on the Oct 24, 2018 ballot, worded by the province, to learn whether residents wanted cannabis sold in Steinbach.
status_detail: The question was on the Oct 24, 2018 ballot (councillors' remarks, 2018-08-07). The July 17 vote is not in the record: the transcript ends before item 9F and no July 17 minutes exist. The plebiscite result is not in the council sources searched.
reasons: protect-residents: Put the question to the public to learn whether cannabis should be for sale in Steinbach. (Jac Siemens)
notes: Also recorded in the health-wellbeing topic. Result of the October 2018 plebiscite not verified from council records.

title: City-serviced industrial lots sell out; few left by 2020
summary: Council sold its remaining small serviced 'incubator' lots on Industrial Road at the $75,000 list price (2018-2019), subdivided Steinbach Community Development Corporation land on Acres Drive for buyers, and approved private industrial and commercial bare-land condos. Sales required building within three years or the city could buy back at 80%; it bought back 88 Acres Drive in Dec 2020 to restock its 'not very many' lots. Mayor Funk said the Acres Drive lots, built with about $1 million in federal money and sold at cost, were all sold by Oct 2019.
status_detail: Sales: 127 Industrial Rd (R18-109), 115 & 119 Industrial Rd (R19-023), 123 Industrial Rd (R19-143); SCDC Acres Drive subdivision (2018-06-19); TCK Holdings lot on Acres Drive (2019-03-19); 15-unit industrial condo at 286 Park Road West (R20-160); buyback of 88 Acres Drive (R19-254 as numbered in minutes, 2020-12-15). By late 2020 councillors described the inventory as very low.
figures: $75,000 per lot (R18-109, R19-143); $150,000 for two (R19-023); about $70,500 net after 6% commission (2019-07-02 1:08:15); buyback $62,400 at 80% of 2017 price (2020-12-15 0:40:22); ~$1 million federal funding for Acres Drive lots (Funk 2019-10-01 0:00:05); 15 condo units on 1.66 acres, ~1,200 sq ft each (2020-08-18 1:19:21, 1:21:04).
mover: John Fehr; Michael Zwaagstra; Susan Penner; Michael Zwaagstra; Jac Siemens
seconder: Jac Siemens; Jac Siemens; Bill Hiebert; Damian Penner; Jake Hiebert
notes: Buyer of 115/119 Industrial Road was an individual (named in minutes); omitted. The 88 Acres Drive resolution is numbered R19-254 in the 2020-12-15 minutes (likely a typo for R20-).

title: Businesses on gravel roads no longer have to pave their parking lots
summary: While adopting the new zoning by-law, council voted 4-2 to require hard-surfaced parking only for sites on paved streets, after complaints that start-up businesses on gravel roads could not afford paving. Mayor Goertzen opposed lowering the city's 'high standard'. Council then excused paving for a distribution business on gravel Park Road West (2018) and, with a one-year condition, for 111 Commerce Drive (2020).
status_detail: R18-128 amended Zoning By-law 2100 s.134.4 (paving required only where a site abuts a paved street or lane); V-2018-24 approved (R18-234, 6-1); V-2020-23 approved with paving due within a year of new construction (R20-175, 5-1).
figures: V-2018-24: 4 required stalls at 266 Park Road West; V-2020-23: paving owed since a 2013 permit (Lumberzone site), outstanding work order from Feb 2, 2015 (minutes).
reasons: cost: Start-ups on gravel roads have lower property values and little money for asphalt; the city's own shop yard is gravel. (John Fehr); fairness-precedent: Like for like: if the city provides a gravel road it should not demand more than gravel. (Earl Funk); protect-residents: Opposed: high, uniform urban standards serve customers and the city long term. (Chris Goertzen)
public: Business owners (Paisley Investments, Three Seventeen Holdings / Superior Projects) asked for relief; no objectors.
mover: John Fehr; Susan Penner; Michael Zwaagstra
seconder: Earl Funk; Michael Zwaagstra; Jake Hiebert
vote: 4-2 (against: Goertzen, C. Penner); 6-1 (against: C. Penner); 5-1 (against: D. Penner)
notes: The Sept 15, 2020 meeting has minutes but no transcript.

title: Concrete company refused permission to run from a 3,000 sq ft home-based shop
summary: S.H. asked to build a 3,000 sq ft shop on a rural residential lot and run a six-person concrete business from it, well over the home-based business limit (25% of floor area or 800 sq ft). Council allowed the large accessory building but refused the home-based business, saying businesses of that size belong in commercial or industrial zones. Fehr pointed to $75,000 incubator lots in the industrial park.
status_detail: R18-124 carried 4-2: accessory building allowed, home-based business at that size denied (against: Goertzen, Fehr).
figures: Home-based business cap: 25% of gross floor area or 800 sq ft; requested 3,000 sq ft shop; 6 employees including 2 owners; incubator lots $75,000 (transcript 0:13:11, 0:20:04, 0:20:20).
reasons: protect-residents: Zoning steers businesses to commercial and industrial areas; home-based businesses are meant to be small with few employees. (Michael Zwaagstra); protect-residents: Noise and dust; a business beyond a "nucleus" should move to a proper zone where it can grow. (Cari Penner (medium-confidence attribution))
public: The applicant S.H. said all mixing is done on site with no concrete trucks and objected to giving up land for a future road.
notes: Applicant named in the minutes; initials used here.

title: Request for a Sunday-shopping vote on the 2018 ballot is turned down 2-5
summary: A former councillor, D.B., asked council in June 2018 to start a dialogue on a by-law letting all retail stores open on Sundays, then asked in writing for a plebiscite at the Oct 24, 2018 election. Councillor Siemens moved a non-binding referendum, saying it would cost nothing extra on the election ballot. Five members voted it down, citing the low threshold (one letter), little public demand, businesses' wish to stay closed, Steinbach's character and the mayor's dislike of governing by referendum. A follow-up petition in September was received as information.
status_detail: R18-184 defeated 2-5 (minutes; the transcript says "Carried" in error). The Sept 18, 2018 petition and plebiscite request from D.B. ("Shop Sunday") was received as information. No by-law to widen Sunday shopping was brought forward in 2018-2020.
figures: A stand-alone vote would cost about $10,000 vs no extra cost on the election ballot (Siemens, transcript 2018-08-07 0:32:10). Provincial exemption cited: businesses with 4 or fewer employees may open (D.B. 2018-06-05 0:56:47; Siemens 0:32:10).
reasons: businesses-support-it: Deferred to business owners he talked to; did not want to put fellow business people in a position where they must open when they do not want to. (John Fehr); fairness-precedent: The threshold for a ballot question would be one letter; the issue rarely comes up at the door; the cannabis question was already on the ballot. (Michael Zwaagstra); market-decides: Partial Sunday shopping has not hindered growth: Steinbach got Superstore and Walmart and rivals Winkler, which also lacks full Sunday shopping. (Michael Zwaagstra (medium-confidence attribution)); fairness-precedent: Had not heard enough of a case or appetite for Sunday shopping to justify the question. (Earl Funk); protect-residents: Residents value Sunday as a family day of rest; it is part of what makes Steinbach unique. (Susan Penner); fairness-precedent: Opposed governing by referendum; council can consult constituents and the Chamber (which had run at least two surveys) and decide itself. (Chris Goertzen)
public: D.B. (former councillor, speaking as a citizen) argued closing rules are inconsistent (restaurants open, grocery stores closed), shift workers drive to Winnipeg on Sundays, and workers' religious days off are already protected by law. He later filed a petition (Sept 2018).
vote: 2-5 (for: Siemens, C. Penner; against: Fehr, Funk, S. Penner, Zwaagstra, Goertzen)
notes: Speaker labels in the 2018-08-07 file are reused across people (label I is both Zwaagstra and Funk); attributions rely on the chair naming the speaker immediately before. Sunday shopping rules are set by provincial law with municipal opt-in by-law; the by-law route was never brought to a vote.

title: Council bends downtown parking rules to fill the empty former credit union building at 305 Main
summary: A church (Calvary Chapel) wanted to lease the long-empty former Steinbach Credit Union building at 305 Main Street but could not supply the 100 parking stalls the zoning by-law required. Against the city manager's advice that developers must provide their own parking, council in July 2018 let it count 52 stalls in the city-shared credit union lot, then in October approved a variance to 10 stalls with conditions. Councillors framed it as downtown vitality: an occupied building on Main Street rather than an empty one or another parking lot.
status_detail: R18-155 (July 3, unanimous) relinquished 52 shared stalls; V-2018-21 (10 stalls instead of 100) approved Oct 2, 2018 with development-agreement conditions (R18-232, unanimous) after two amendments to lighten the conditions failed 3-4.
figures: 100 stalls required for a 400-seat assembly area; variance to 10 (minutes 2018-10-02); 52 stalls in the shared credit union lot (R18-155); proposed annual payment $5,200 (amendment R18-230).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Worried it signals exceptions for favoured organizations; preferred a variance with a public hearing. (John Fehr); study-first: Advised that the developer provide its own parking and that council study implications before transferring public parking. (Troy Warkentin)
public: Calvary Chapel's delegation said the building had sat empty for years and that leasing it would take a "for lease" sign off Main Street; minor hockey raised parking concerns in a letter (Aug 2018).
vote: unanimous (R18-155, Fehr appears to abstain in the transcript); R18-232 unanimous after amendments R18-230/R18-231 defeated 3-4
notes: This case concerns a church, but council debated it as a test of downtown parking rules for any business. Fehr's abstention on R18-155 is from the transcript only.

title: Councillors call for a review of downtown parking requirements; relief comes case by case instead
summary: During the 305 Main debate (July 2018) and when adopting the new zoning by-law (Oct 2018), councillors said downtown parking rules were too strict, noting 25 to 30 Main Street businesses did not comply. No review was brought back in 2018-2020; instead council kept granting variances, e.g. a gym and training business at 306 Main Street in June 2019 was required to arrange 7 of 30 stalls.
status_detail: Siemens asked a future council to do a complete central business district parking review (Oct 16, 2018). No review or by-law amendment was found through 2020; V-2019-16 (R19-134) reduced 306 Main's requirement from 30 to 7 stalls.
figures: 25 to 30 Main Street businesses not compliant with parking rules (Funk, 2018-07-03 0:44:45); 306 Main: 7 of 30 required stalls, 2 can be on-street (R19-134; Funk 2019-06-18 0:28:08).
reasons: study-first: Flagged a full parking review for the next council rather than changing the rules during the zoning by-law adoption. (Jac Siemens)
notes: Whether a later council reviewed CBD parking is outside this period (the 2022-2026 report notes a one-third parking cut downtown).

title: Council buys three more Hanover Street lots to finish a downtown land block
summary: Following a strategy of about 25 years, council bought 336 Hanover ($194,500), 332 Hanover ($172,900) and 380 Hanover ($280,000) next to the T.G. Smith Centre, renting the houses until a use is chosen. Supporters named a hotel, multifamily housing, mixed use, parking or commercial development as possible future uses. Councillor Fehr voted against all three, saying the city was over budget, residents did not support the planned downtown development and business people feared being bought out.
status_detail: All three purchases carried, each with Fehr alone against (R18-152, R18-174, R18-238). Cari Penner called 380 Hanover "the last key piece". In Oct 2019 council offered this land for the proposed downtown event centre (see 2019-downtown-event-centre-mou).
figures: 336 Hanover $194,500 (R18-152); 332 Hanover $172,900 (R18-174); 380 Hanover $280,000, possession June 26, 2019 (R18-238); city already owned two lots north and two south of 380 (Warkentin, 2018-10-16 0:28:30).
mover: Earl Funk; Cari Penner; Cari Penner
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra; Susan Penner; Susan Penner
notes: Fehr's claim that business people feared being bought out is his own report; not verified.

title: First third-party digital advertising sign on Main Street approved 6-1
summary: Signex Manufacturing applied for a digital sign at 352 Main Street that could carry third-party advertising, a first for the central business district. Siemens noted it set a precedent but voted for it; Cari Penner voted against, asking what council wanted the downtown to look like. Zwaagstra and Fehr said digital advertising is simply how businesses advertise now.
status_detail: Conditional use CU-2018-05 approved (R18-204), 6-1, Cari Penner against. No downtown sign policy review followed in the period.
reasons: fairness-precedent: Precedent for more digital signs downtown; council should first decide how it wants the CBD to look. (Cari Penner)
public: The applicant (Signex Manufacturing) said the owner could advertise suppliers or others on the sign.
notes: Mover/seconder differ between minutes (Zwaagstra/Fehr) and transcript (Fehr moved, Siemens seconded); minutes used for the decision record.

title: Mayor tasks the city's development corporation with economic development; "Why Steinbach" site launched
summary: After the 2018 election, Mayor Funk tasked the Steinbach Community Development Corporation (city-controlled, Susan Penner as council representative) with starting economic development work. In June 2019 Penner presented the 'Why Steinbach' investor website (growth data, available land, zoning, direct contact with the mayor and CAO), a billboard east of Kenora, talks with the Chamber, Red River College (trades and health-care aide training) and the airport.
status_detail: Website live June 18, 2019 (presented as information). Susan Penner re-appointed SCDC representative Nov 5, 2019 and Nov 3, 2020. The college and airport talks were described as preliminary; no results reported in 2019-2020.
figures: SCDC received no city grant in 2018 or 2019 ($0 in the grants lists, R19-073, R20-064) vs $239,655.24 in 2017 (R18-065; purpose not stated).

title: Council points to building permits and infrastructure as its economic development strategy
summary: Councillors repeatedly answered calls for economic development by pointing to growth: $57 million in permits in 2018, about $81 million in 2019 ($46 million commercial), $720 million over 2009-2019 with 55% commercial, and $100-115 million in infrastructure. They approved commercial variances quickly ('we're open for business') but created no incentives, grants or dedicated economic development staff in 2018-2020.
status_detail: No incentive program, tax break or economic development office was created in the period; the approach was infrastructure, land, quick approvals and the SCDC website.
figures: 2018 permits just under $57 million (Funk 2019-01-15 1:08:03); 2019 permits ~$81 million incl. ~$46 million commercial (Funk 2020-01-07 2:13:50); 2009-2019 permits $720,997,744.60, 55% commercial; infrastructure 2009-2018 $100,719,684 (S. Penner 2020-01-21 0:00:17); commercial/industrial 33.5% of assessment (assessor, 2019-06-04).
reasons: market-decides: Steinbach has thrived for a decade; infrastructure investment is what attracts business. (Susan Penner); market-decides: Creating a climate for growth is working. (Earl Funk)
notes: The 2019 building-permit total quoted by the mayor is from the transcript; verify against permit reports if published.

title: New council questions the Chamber pass-through and promises a review; tax continues unchanged
summary: At the April 2019 business tax vote, Susan Penner asked why the city funds the Chamber and said a large operating grant could compromise a chamber that should lobby for lower business taxes. Mayor Funk said he had been 'conflicted' from the start and the arrangement should be looked at. In June 2019 Penner said the July study session would decide whether the business tax continues. No public decision followed; the 0.5% tax and grant continued in 2020.
status_detail: Review promised (Apr 2019) and placed on a July 2019 study session per Susan Penner; no public outcome found. The 2020 levy passed unchanged (By-law 2151).
reasons: businesses-support-it: Kept it because the Chamber brings added (or perceived) value to the business community; an abrupt change would shock people. (Earl Funk); study-first: Supported the levy but wanted a review or presentation on the arrangement. (Susan Penner)
notes: Study sessions are not public; outcome inferred only from the unchanged 2020 levy. In 2021 (outside this period) the city and Chamber set up a jointly funded economic development office.

title: Thrift store allowed in a light industrial zone, case by case
summary: Retail is only a conditional use in the M1 light industrial zone. Council approved Local Matters Thrift Store (a nonprofit) at 92 PTH 52 West, already operating for months, citing the Meadow Mart precedent and no conflicts.
status_detail: CU-2019-02 approved subject to an occupancy permit (R19-133, unanimous).
public: The store manager said it had outgrown its Acres Drive location.
notes: Compare the 2022-2026 report, where council protected the subsidized industrial park from retail.

title: Council backs a $42.5 million downtown event centre on its assembled land
summary: Council signed a memorandum of understanding with Southeast Event Centre Inc., a nonprofit of local business people, for a 2,500-seat event centre and 500-seat hall beside the T.G. Smith Centre on city-assembled downtown land. The city pledged $10 million and land, SEC at least $15 million in donations, and the city applied for $17.5 million from federal and provincial programs. Council framed it as keeping downtown vibrant and drawing regional visitors.
status_detail: MOU approved (R19-193) and grant application authorized (R19-198), both unanimous. The project depended on senior-government funding; no funding decision appears in the 2019-2020 record.
figures: Total $42.5 million: city $10 million, SEC $15 million+, grant request $17.5 million (Funk 2019-10-01 0:29:08); 2,500 seats, up to 3,200 for floor events; 500-seat hall (presentation and Zwaagstra 0:33:01).
reasons: partner-money: Project proceeds only with funding from other levels of government. (Earl Funk)
public: Southeast Event Centre Inc. presented (organization).
notes: Primarily a recreation project; included here for its downtown and land-assembly links.

title: 20-acre Millbrook Market commercial mixed-use plan approved on PTH 12 North
summary: A local developer group (10027732 Manitoba Inc.) proposed Millbrook Market, about 20 acres beside Superstore with 60-70% retail, office and possibly big-box commercial and 30-40% multifamily. Council adopted the secondary plan and rezoned the land from development reserve to the new commercial mixed-use (CMX) zone, praising private developers for innovative projects. Follow-up variances for its residential setbacks were dealt with in 2020.
status_detail: By-law 2136 (secondary plan) and 2137 (rezoning to CMX) passed unanimously (R20-007/008, R20-042 to R20-045). Variances for the site were heard May 5 and Oct 20, 2020.
figures: About 20 acres; 60-70% commercial, 30-40% multifamily (presentation 2020-03-03 0:18:55).
reasons: market-decides: The best projects come from private developers, not government. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: D.B. presented for the developer; no objections to this file.
mover: Michael Zwaagstra; Jake Hiebert; Jac Siemens; Michael Zwaagstra
seconder: Jac Siemens; Bill Hiebert; Damian Penner; Damian Penner
notes: D.B. is the same former councillor who requested the Sunday shopping vote in 2018; identified by initials as a member of the public.

title: COVID-19: council lobbies the province to reopen business, but offers no local relief
summary: In April 2020 Mayor Funk and Susan Penner met the Chamber; businesses were asked for their COVID stories, and the city sent the Premier a letter (drafted by the deputy mayor) with a Chamber support letter and the stories on April 14. In June the mayor sent a second letter urging faster reopening of retail and restaurants and full church capacity; councillors spoke strongly for lifting restrictions. No city-level business relief (tax or fee deferral, patio program, grants) appears in the 2020 transcripts or minutes.
status_detail: Both letters sent; the province announced reopening April 29 (Phase 1 from May 4, including restaurant patios). The $947,678.60 federal-provincial Safe Restart grant (Nov 2020) was to be put in a reserve for a project, not a business program.
figures: Safe Restart allocation $947,678.60 (Funk 2020-11-03 1:26:28).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: The municipal role is to be a voice to the province for reopening, not to add local restrictions. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Local businesses supplied impact stories via the Chamber (not published).
notes: No patio, sidewalk-sale or fee-relief measure was found in council records for 2020; patios were reopened under provincial orders. Minutes of May 19 and Nov 17, 2020 are missing.

title: Truck dealer refused a waiver from street-edge tree planting, 4-3
summary: Steinbach Truck Services asked to skip all required street-edge trees and shrubs at 435 PTH 12 North so its product could be seen from the road. Administration warned of a precedent. Siemens, Susan Penner and Bill Hiebert supported the waiver (gravel road, reduced city services, business plans change); Zwaagstra, Jake Hiebert, Damian Penner and Mayor Funk refused, noting the business had submitted a plan with the trees.
status_detail: Approval (R20-197) defeated 3-4; denial (R20-198) carried 4-3.
figures: Requirement: one tree per 30 ft and three shrubs per 20 ft of frontage, in the by-law since about 2010 (Warkentin 0:30:06, 0:32:41).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Requirement in place since 2010; the applicant knew and had submitted a plan with the trees; applicant absent to explain. (Michael Zwaagstra); protect-residents: Not convinced planting trees would be a hardship; values trees at the city entrance. (Earl Funk)
public: Applicant (Wostco Contractors for Steinbach Truck Services) did not attend; no objectors.
vote: approve defeated 3-4; deny carried 4-3 (for denial: Zwaagstra, J. Hiebert, D. Penner, Funk; against: Siemens, S. Penner, B. Hiebert)

title: Truck dealership and service centre approved at the north entrance
summary: Council approved a conditional use at 1340 Northgate Drive for fleet services so a company affiliated with Freightliner Manitoba could build a 20,000+ sq ft dealership, service and parts facility. Councillors welcomed the full-time, well-paying jobs.
status_detail: CU-2020-10 carried (transcript); Nov 17, 2020 minutes not available, so no resolution number.
figures: First phase over 20,000 sq ft (applicant's representative, 0:58:50).
public: Representatives of the owner and buyer (B.S., W.E.) spoke for it; no objectors.

title: Acres Drive extension to open more industrial park land, paid by frontage levy
summary: Council gave first reading to a $3.1 million local improvement to build about 500 m of Acres Drive with a water main from Industrial Road to Keating Road, continuing the industrial park. Frontage owners pay: the city's Steinbach Community Development Corporation and Envision Community Living, a charity that objected it gains nothing. Council held to a 2007 development agreement and its no-exceptions practice; Siemens voted against.
status_detail: First reading only (R20-251, 5-1) in this period; later readings and construction fall after Dec 2020.
figures: About 500 lineal metres; estimated debt and borrowing $3.1 million (Warkentin 2020-12-15 0:06:32).
reasons: fairness-precedent: All properties on a local improvement pay by frontage; exempting a nonprofit would be a first and a precedent. (Michael Zwaagstra); partner-money: Land sale proceeds return to the SCDC, which reinvests them in roads that open more land. (Earl Funk)
public: Envision Community Living (J.D., J.D.) said the levy diverts charity funds, its Eastman Recycling site uses Industrial Road access, and notice came during a pandemic code red.
notes: The two Envision speakers share the initials J.D.

title: Record building permits, with commercial and institutional construction leading in 2023
summary: Monthly permit reports showed strong growth: about $94.5 million by late 2021, then a record 2023 that passed $182 million by mid-October and over $200 million for the year, with commercial, industrial and institutional work (including the event centre, hospital expansion and a new school) making up most of it.
status_detail: Monthly permit lists accepted each month (routine).
figures: 2020 total $66,359,629 (mayor, Jan 19, 2021); 2021 year to date $94.5M at Dec 7, 2021 (mayor); 2023 $182M by Oct 17 (Susan Penner) and over $200M for the year, around 70% commercial (Siemens, Dec 19, 2023).
notes: "Commercial" in these reports includes institutional projects such as the event centre, hospital and school.

title: City sells long-listed industrial land and approves private industrial subdivisions
summary: Council sold 45 Tower Avenue (about 20 acres in the Hespeler industrial park, for sale for years) at its listed price and resold 88 Acres Drive, a lot it had just bought back from an owner who had not built. It also approved a private subdivision of 95 Industrial Road into three lots. Councillors said industrial land inventory was getting low; Jac Siemens asked whether the city's two-year build requirement still applied.
status_detail: Sales and subdivision approved; the subdivision was re-approved as amended on Feb 16, 2021 (R21-040).
figures: 45 Tower Ave sold for $645,900 (R21-023); 88 Acres Dr sold for $124,900 (R21-024) after the city bought it back for $62,400 in Dec 2020 (R19-254 as numbered in the parsed minutes).
mover: Jac Siemens (R21-023); Susan Penner (R21-024); Damian Penner (R21-028); Michael Zwaagstra (R21-040)
seconder: Susan Penner (R21-023); Michael Zwaagstra (R21-024); Jake Hiebert (R21-028, R21-040)
notes: "Steinac" and "Steinbach" are transcript renderings of Steinbach.

title: Council commits $65,000 a year for five years to a Chamber-run economic development office
summary: After a Chamber of Commerce proposal in fall 2020, council adopted terms of reference to match private funding for an economic development office run by the Chamber, to a maximum of $65,000 a year for 2021–2025. The Chamber directs the office, councillors are kept off its committee, and the Chamber must report to the city twice a year on "development results and benefits".
status_detail: Funded from 2021; the Chamber grant line rose accordingly. The terms set no measurable targets (jobs, investments, land sales). Public reports to council in this period came only on Oct 18, 2022 and Jul 18, 2023, not twice a year; any other reporting was not in a recorded meeting.
figures: Up to $65,000/yr matching grant, 2021–2025; renewal proposal due by Jun 30, 2025 (R21-049, minutes). Chamber grant total $130,705.54 (2020) → $192,669.87 (2021) (R22-066) → $208,542.20 (2022) (R23-039); these totals combine the business-tax pass-through and the economic development grant.
public: The proposal came from the Steinbach Chamber of Commerce and a group of private investors; no residents spoke.
notes: Pre-2022 speakers identified from minutes and how the mayor addresses them (no speaker map). "Standby" is the transcript's rendering of "Steinbach". The 2025 end of the funding is outside this period.

title: City's development corporation subdivides new 1.5- to 2.5-acre industrial lots
summary: Through the Steinbach Community Development Corporation (the city's land company, on whose board Susan Penner and the mayor sat), council created two lots on Industrial Road (2021), three 2-acre lots on the new Acres Drive extension with Industrial Road West renamed Campbell Drive (Oct 2022), and four 1.5-acre lots further along Acres Drive (Dec 2022). Councillors said small lots sell fast and supply was low.
status_detail: Nine new city lots created in the period, plus a 10-acre residual parcel kept for larger users. Prices and sales were not discussed in open meetings. SCDC's 2020 financial report was accepted Jul 20, 2021 (R21-159).
figures: 2 lots of about 2 and 2.5 acres (Mar 16, 2021, R21-058); 3 lots of about 2 acres plus a residual parcel of about 10.5 acres (Oct 4, 2022, R22-223); 4 lots of 1.5 acres (Dec 6, 2022; no minutes found).
resolution_no: R21-058, R22-223, By-law 2166; Dec 6, 2022 subdivision (no minutes found)
mover: Jake Hiebert (R21-058); Damian Penner (R22-223); Bill Hiebert (Dec 6, 2022, transcript)
seconder: Damian Penner (R21-058); Jake Hiebert (R22-223); Damian Penner (Dec 6, 2022, transcript)
notes: Dec 6, 2022 has no minutes or speaker map; mover/seconder taken from the transcript (Siemens, Jake Hiebert and Susan Penner were excused).

title: Acres Drive extended to open new industrial lots, paid without borrowing
summary: Council pushed a local improvement to extend Acres Drive (concrete street and water main) from Industrial Road West to Keating Road because industrial lot inventory was low. One objection sent it to the Municipal Board, which approved it; construction was tendered in 2022. In December 2022 council cancelled the $3.1 million borrowing authority because the project came in well under estimate and the Steinbach Community Development Corporation had funds to cover it.
status_detail: Built in summer 2022 (Friesen Hauling); new city lots were subdivided along it in Oct and Dec 2022. Borrowing authority cancelled by By-law 2219 (first and second readings Dec 6, 2022; third reading R23-040, Feb 21, 2023).
figures: Borrowing authority up to $3.1M (city manager, Apr 20, 2021, 0:25:52; Zwaagstra, Feb 15, 2022); tender awarded to Friesen Hauling Inc. for $1,645,544.40 plus taxes (R22-078, Apr 5, 2022).
public: One objection was filed (not identified in the record) and heard by the Municipal Board on Sep 9, 2021.
mover: Susan Penner (R21-081); Michael Zwaagstra (R22-044); Jake Hiebert (R22-078)
seconder: Damian Penner (R21-081); Susan Penner (R22-044); Damian Penner (R22-078)
notes: No speaker map or minutes exist for Dec 6, 2022 (no resolution numbers); speakers identified from the transcript. Siemens's Dec 2020 vote against first reading is outside this period and his reasons are not reviewed here.

title: Business tax kept at 0.5% each year and passed to the Chamber of Commerce
summary: Council renewed the 0.5% business tax by by-law each spring (By-laws 2172, 2208, 2226), all unanimous, describing it as an "in and out": the city collects it and gives it to the Chamber, which relies on it to operate. Susan Penner noted the Chamber gets more each year as businesses are added. In July 2023 the Chamber asked for a motion transferring its grant; Michael Zwaagstra said council would decide later.
status_detail: Levied at 0.5% in 2021, 2022 and 2023. No service agreement, deliverables or cap on the Chamber's share were discussed in recorded meetings.
figures: Rate 0.5% (city manager, May 4, 2021, 0:32:33; May 3, 2022, 0:06:23); was about 1% some 15 years earlier (Zwaagstra, May 3, 2022). Chamber grant totals $130,705.54 (2020), $192,669.87 (2021), $208,542.20 (2022) (R22-066, R23-039, including the economic development grant).
public: The Chamber presented a "business tax grant" delegation on Jul 18, 2023 (C.B.).
notes: Budget grant discussions are not recorded. The May 16, 2023 second-reading speaker (map: Bill Hiebert) conflicts with the minutes mover (Jake Hiebert); not quoted.

title: Downtown microbrewery and gallery allowed with 5 parking stalls instead of 11
summary: The Public Brewhouse and Gallery asked to open at 301 Main Street with 5 on-site stalls instead of the 11 required, citing off-peak hours, walkability and the downtown plan's goal of more restaurants and entertainment. Council approved without requiring replacement parking elsewhere, citing two earlier downtown parking variances.
status_detail: Variance V-2021-10 approved unanimously, dropping administration's suggested condition of alternate stalls.
figures: 5 stalls instead of 11 (city manager, 0:07:12).
public: S.C. spoke for the applicant; no objections at the hearing (5 letters were received, content not read out).

title: Rezoning of a church property in the industrial park for a school refused
summary: A church on Life Science Parkway (allowed years earlier by conditional use) asked to rezone from light industrial to educational-institutional to run a school. Administration recommended refusal because industrial infrastructure is not built for schools. Susan Penner and Jac Siemens wanted a public hearing; the majority refused first reading to keep the land industrial permanently.
status_detail: First reading of By-law 2170 defeated 2-5, then first reading denied 5-2.
reasons: fairness-precedent: rezoning is permanent and would allow any school there later; poor planning (Michael Zwaagstra); protect-residents: industrial area not built for children's foot and bike traffic; future councils would pay for sidewalks (Damian Penner)
public: The applicant (a church) is not named in the record reviewed; no one spoke at this first-reading stage.
vote: R21-090 defeated 2-5 (for: S. Penner, J. Siemens); R21-091 carried 5-2 (against: S. Penner, J. Siemens)
notes: A councillor addressed as "Councillor Heaver" (0:23:52) also opposed a school in the industrial area, but the label (F) is Siemens elsewhere in this file, so the turn is not attributed.

title: Third-party advertising signs allowed in light-industrial zones by conditional use
summary: Council amended the zoning by-law so advertising signs can be approved as a conditional use in the M-1 light-industrial zone, as already allowed in commercial and heavy-industrial zones, then approved an electronic message sign with third-party advertising for a multi-tenant building at 132 Industrial Road.
status_detail: By-law 2175 passed; CU-2021-02 approved. Each sign still needs council approval.
public: P.R. of Signex Manufacturing spoke for the applicant (AirMaster Mechanical's building); no objections.
seconder: Damian Penner, Jac Siemens, Bill Hiebert (by-law readings); Damian Penner (CU-2021-02)

title: Variances granted so businesses can build or open (setbacks, parking, hotel addition)
summary: Council routinely granted business variances: a zero front setback for a commercial/office building on Loewen Boulevard (2021, over a neighbouring business owner's traffic concerns), 3 parking stalls instead of 4 for a new Mexican grocery on PTH 52 West (2021), and a reduced side yard for a Days Inn addition (2022). Councillors said the city should not stop a business over one parking stall.
status_detail: All granted; the grocery variance was conditional on 3 stalls fitting and lapses if the building expands.
figures: Adding a stall would have cost the grocery applicant "over $120,000" by his estimate (applicant, Sep 21, 2021).
public: Applicants: M.F. (Loewen Blvd building), J.F. (grocery), E.S. for Schinkel Properties (Days Inn). A neighbouring business owner objected to the Loewen Blvd variance over traffic and access; another neighbour objected to the hotel addition.
vote: R21-114 6-1 (against: J. Hiebert); R21-198 and R22-238 unanimous

title: Sidewalk patios approved for Main Street restaurants
summary: Council approved seasonal sidewalk patios for Chicken Chef (365 Main St, 2021) and Di Reggae Grill (254 Main St, 2022), following a Sonny Beans patio in place since 2010. Each needs an annual permit, must keep the sidewalk clear, and can be revoked by the city. Councillors said patios make downtown more vibrant and invited other businesses to apply.
status_detail: Both approved unanimously; handled one by one by resolution rather than through a standing patio program or policy.
figures: Chicken Chef walkway uses 2 parking stalls (Adam Thiessen, Jun 1, 2021, 0:54:24).
public: Requests came from the restaurant owners (letters).

title: New commercial and commercial-mixed-use land designated in large developments
summary: Council redesignated and rezoned land for commercial and commercial mixed-use (CMX) uses in new developments: the front of a 67-acre parcel on Park Road West near Clearspring Mall (2021) and a corner at Old Tom Road and Loewen Boulevard (2022–2023), citing the success of Millbrook Market. Residents raised drainage and traffic concerns; councillors welcomed the investment.
status_detail: Plan amendments and rezonings passed (Old Tom/Loewen third readings Jun 6, 2023 after ministerial approval).
public: Several nearby residents objected to the Loewen Blvd/Old Tom Road plan over drainage and traffic (Sep 6, 2022).
notes: Grouped routine land-use readings; residents are not named.

title: Retail in the industrial park: two narrow approvals, one broad request denied
summary: Council approved a clothing retailer in one unit at 94 Industrial Road (April 2022, 5-2), unanimously denied blanket retail for a whole multi-unit site at 110 Industrial Road (October 2022), then approved occasional charity book sales by ROC Eastman in two units of the same site, limited to that tenant (November 2022, 5-2). Majority reasoning: industrial parks are subsidized for industry, retail belongs in commercial areas, and council must keep control unit by unit.
status_detail: Narrow, conditioned approvals (major occupancy agreement; tied to a single tenant) and one denial. Jake Hiebert suggested rezoning the area if retail keeps being approved; no rezoning followed in this period.
reasons: fairness-precedent: industrial parks are subsidized to attract industry; retail goes to unsubsidized commercial land (Michael Zwaagstra); fairness-precedent: subsidized industrial space undercuts developers who built commercial space (Susan Penner); fairness-precedent: blanket approval would hand council's decision to the landlord (Jac Siemens); fairness-precedent: retail is retail, light industrial is light industrial; rezone the area if needed (Jake Hiebert); fairness-precedent: tenant-specific conditions may not hold as the charity changes (Damian Penner)
public: Applicants: H.B. and Skirts and Co. owners (94 Industrial Rd, minutes); S.H., landlord of 110 Industrial Rd; ROC Eastman (charity). S.H. pointed to other retail already on Industrial Road (Lumber Zone, Concrete Source and others).
vote: R22-077 5-2 (against: Zwaagstra, J. Hiebert); R22-224 unanimous (deny); R22-262 5-2 (against: D. Penner, J. Hiebert)
notes: The Apr 5, 2022 video has no audio, so reasons for the Skirts and Co. votes come from the minutes only. In the Oct 4, 2022 file, a merged Hiebert label (low) states opposition to retail in industrial areas; not quoted.

title: Damian Penner criticizes the province's move away from inflation-linked minimum wage increases
summary: In his opening remarks, Damian Penner, speaking also as an employer, argued that Bill 44 would make minimum wage a political rather than inflation-based decision, could cut entry-level jobs, and that the province should instead raise the personal tax exemption.
status_detail: Opening remarks only; council took no position or action.
reasons: provincial-responsibility: province should cut taxes on low earners rather than put the onus on businesses (Damian Penner)

title: Strip of public reserve sold so Priority Auto can expand on Acres Drive
summary: A business at 60 Acres Drive asked to buy a small strip of public reserve (about 49 m by 6 m) to expand. Administration found no drainage or development problem and council agreed; the reserve was formally closed by By-law 2218 in 2023.
status_detail: Sale approved subject to consolidation with 60 Acres Drive; By-law 2218 third reading Mar 21, 2023 (R23-062).
notes: The seconder's supporting remarks (0:26:26) come from a merged Hiebert label (low confidence) and are not quoted.

title: Chamber reports on the new Steinbach Economic Development corporation and an investment-attraction study
summary: In the first public report on the office, Chamber chair C.B. said the economic development office had been incorporated as Steinbach Economic Development (separate from the city's Community Development Corporation, which manages city land), had commissioned an investment-attraction study and workforce assessment from ROI (Research on Investment), and that the Chamber's executive director would become its director. Jake Hiebert asked who from the business community oversees the office.
status_detail: Received as information. The study was presented in July 2023 (see 2023-sed-strategy). The offered council seat on the new corporation's board was left "to discuss further"; no decision found.
figures: 26 private stakeholders fund and oversee the office; Chamber, immigrant services and economic development staff total about 20 (delegation, 0:43:09).
public: C.B. (Chamber chair) presented; M.B. (Chamber executive director, incoming director of economic development) attended. The Chamber also described job fairs for Ukrainian newcomers and short-term housing for refugees close to securing work.

title: Industrial remnant beside Loewen Windows redesignated for downtown apartments over the company's objection
summary: A developer asked to move part of 78 PTH 52 West from industrial to central business district and rezone for a 22–24 unit, 3-storey apartment on First Street. Loewen Windows, a major employer across the intersection, objected on traffic, staff safety and sightlines. The majority said the small strip had no industrial future and housing near jobs was good; Jac Siemens and Jake Hiebert voted against, Siemens saying the downtown district was meant for business and wanting a 30-foot highway buffer.
status_detail: Second readings carried 5-2; the plan amendment went to the minister for approval. Later readings are outside this review.
figures: 22–24 units, 3 storeys (city manager, 0:40:58).
reasons: not-council-role: council approves the concept; detailed design is administration's job (Susan Penner); market-decides: strip has no future industrial use; traffic lights already requested (Damian Penner)
public: J.S. spoke for Loewen Windows against both by-laws (traffic and pedestrian safety at PTH 52 and Giesbrecht, sightlines, appearance). Residents also raised noise and sightlines.
notes: The delegate's company is named; the speaker is identified by initials only.

title: Park Road West paved through to Industrial Road, linking to the north commercial area
summary: Council used reserves to extend paving of Park Road West about 260 metres beyond a developer's section so it connects to Industrial Road, giving another route to the north-end commercial district.
status_detail: Tender awarded.
figures: Friesen Hauling Ltd., $1,970,097 plus taxes (R23-057); about 260 m (mayor, 0:52:21).

title: Steinbach Economic Development presents its agribusiness-focused strategy
summary: M.B., director of Steinbach Economic Development since January 2023, presented the ROI asset evaluation: 22 stakeholder interviews, a "holistic" approach (business expansion and attraction, quality of life, workforce) and agribusiness, food processing and logistics as the lead sector. The mayor said he and Susan Penner had been asked to help shape the plan. Councillors asked no questions about targets or results.
status_detail: Received as information; no targets or reporting measures were adopted by council in this period. The same evening the Chamber asked for a motion transferring its grant; council deferred it to budget grant discussions.
figures: Pilot runs 2021–2025 (M.B., 0:26:21); 22 stakeholder interviews, including 8 operator interviews (0:26:21).
public: M.B. (director, Steinbach Economic Development) and C.B. (Chamber president) presented.
notes: Speaker C at 0:39:48 cannot be named with confidence; by elimination it is likely Jake Hiebert (unverified).

title: Provincial economic development infrastructure grant sought for Hespeler Street industrial corridor
summary: Council applied to Manitoba's new Municipal Economic Development Infrastructure Program (MEDIP) for half the cost of renewing Hespeler Street, which Damian Penner called an industrial corridor with recent land sales, plus Hanover Street and a fire hall ventilation project.
status_detail: Applications approved by council; no grant result found in council transcripts or motions for 2024–2025.
figures: Hespeler St: $1,660,000 grant requested, $3,320,000 total (R23-200); Hanover St: $560,000 of $1,120,000 (R23-201); fire hall: $300,000 of $400,000 (R23-202). Program about $46M province-wide (city manager, 0:20:52, "in the neighborhood").
mover: Damian Penner (R23-200); Bill Hiebert (R23-201); Michael Zwaagstra (R23-202)
seconder: Susan Penner (R23-200); Jac Siemens (R23-201); Damian Penner (R23-202)
notes: Grant outcome not verified.

title: Development fees, including non-residential fees, raised 5% a year instead of the 7.5% staff proposed
summary: Administration proposed raising residential and non-residential capital development fees and sewer and water impact fees by 7.5% a year for 2024–2027, combined in one by-law, because fees had risen only 2.5% a year since 2012 while construction costs rose 5–6%. Michael Zwaagstra amended it to 5% to keep building affordable. Damian Penner and Jake Hiebert voted against at every reading because they wanted the higher 7.5% so growth would not shift costs to existing taxpayers.
status_detail: By-law 2233 passed at 5% a year for four years (to be reviewed in 2027); smaller than the increase administration recommended.
figures: Previous increases 2.5%/yr since 2012; construction inflation about 5–6%/yr (Zwaagstra, Oct 17, 2023, 0:08:47); SPC notes said about 11%/yr would be needed to restore past contribution levels (Damian Penner, Nov 7, 2023, 0:07:13).
reasons: cost: every increase is passed on to buyers; err on the side of affordability and encourage development (Michael Zwaagstra); cost: would not have supported 7.5%; costs are passed on to consumers (Susan Penner); cost: 5% ties to inflation; other governments are trying to cut housing costs (Earl Funk); cost: too big an increase could hurt the growth rate (Jac Siemens); fairness-precedent: existing taxpayers subsidize developers when fees fall short (argued for more, not less) (Jake Hiebert); fairness-precedent: residents pay either through fees or the mill rate; fees should cover their budget line (argued for more) (Damian Penner)
public: No public delegations.
seconder: Jac Siemens (R23-211); Bill Hiebert (R23-224); Susan Penner (R23-225)
vote: 5-2 at each reading (against: D. Penner, J. Hiebert)
notes: Strategic Priorities Committee (Sep 12, 2023) discussion is not recorded.

title: Truck yard at 45 Tower Avenue refused next to homes
summary: A trucking business asked for a conditional use to run a freight/truck yard on a city-developed industrial lot in the Hespeler industrial park (M-1), plus a variance for barbed wire. Neighbours filed about 17 letters. Council said it wanted the business but refused both because the whole lot backs onto homes.
status_detail: CU-2023-02 denied (R24-009) and barbed-wire variance V-2023-25 denied (R24-010), both unanimous.
figures: About 17 pieces of correspondence (City Manager, transcript 0:46:03); applicant proposed developing 4 acres (transcript 1:23:14).
reasons: protect-residents: Wants the business to proceed but a truck yard is not compatible next to the neighbourhood; work had started before approval. (Michael Zwaagstra); protect-residents: Approval would run with the whole lot, so truck activity could grow right up to the residential line. (Damian Penner)
public: Neighbouring residents objected over noise, dust, lights and 24-hour truck traffic (several speakers and about 17 letters). The applicant (S.S.) said only part of the lot would be used.
notes: Applicant named in the City Manager introduction; given by initials here.

title: Economic development office reports; council asks how success will be measured
summary: In year four of the five-year pilot, Steinbach Economic Development (SED) presented its strategy (advanced agribusiness; four target sectors; foreign-investment grant from Global Affairs Canada). Deputy Mayor Zwaagstra asked for markers of success; SED said targets had been set but would follow up. SED said serviced land is a disadvantage for attracting large investors.
status_detail: Received as information. No targets were reported back on the public record before council ended funding in Aug 2025.
figures: Pilot runs to end of 2025 (C.B., transcript 0:20:09); 4 target sectors: food processing and manufacturing, agribusiness inputs, wholesale trade and distribution, agritech (transcript 0:30:08).
public: SED director M.B. and SED president C.B. presented. M.B. said investors need serviced land, not just available land, and that Steinbach is at a disadvantage on it. A large manufacturer lead through the province had not gone further.
notes: Delegates identified by initials. SED said it incorporated partly to reach funding the Chamber could not (minutes).

title: Main-floor commercial requirements waived when tenants can't be found
