summary: Council twice let developers drop or cut required main-floor commercial space: at 330 First Street (Mar 2024, all residential) and at 31 Loewen Boulevard, where council approved a four-storey mixed-use building with over 10,000 sq ft of commercial in Jan 2026 and then, in Oct 2026, let the developer replace most of it with apartments after failing to find tenants. Councillor Jake Hiebert voiced concern that the second project had become an apartment block in a commercial zone.
status_detail: V-2024-02 approved (R24-063, unanimous); CU-2025-06 and V-2025-38 approved (R26-003, R26-004); V-2026-21 carried Oct 20, 2026 (transcript; minutes not yet available, vote not recorded).
figures: 330 First St: 15 units, 3 storeys (J. Hiebert 2:13:26). 31 Loewen Blvd: 33 units and over 10,000 sq ft commercial (City Manager, 2026-01-06 0:13:31); Oct 2026: one ~1,800–1,900 sq ft commercial unit plus about 6 more suites (applicant, 2026-10-20 0:07:10).
reasons: market-decides: Developers know what the market wants; less commercial is what the area needs. (Mayor Earl Funk); market-decides: 2024: developer tried and found no commercial tenants. (Jake Hiebert)
public: Developers (W.N. in 2024; N.T. for Three Way Builders in 2026) said they could not lease main-floor commercial space; N.T. said tenants will not wait 12–14 months for construction and there may be excess commercial capacity. No objections.
resolution_no: R24-063; R26-003; R26-004; V-2026-21 (no resolution number yet)
mover: Jake Hiebert (R24-063); Damian Penner (R26-003); Michael Zwaagstra (R26-004); Susan Penner (V-2026-21, transcript)
seconder: Jac Siemens (R24-063); Michael Zwaagstra (R26-003); Bill Hiebert (R26-004); "Councillor Bill Pinner" as heard (V-2026-21)
vote: unanimous (2024, Jan 2026); Oct 2026 carried, no recorded vote
notes: Oct 20, 2026 minutes were not available; mover per transcript; the councillor who argued for "matching the approval process with market demand" (label G, 0:10:52) is unidentified (likely Zwaagstra, not confirmed). The seconder was heard as "Councilor Bill Pinner".

title: 0.5% business tax renewed each year and passed to the Chamber of Commerce
summary: Each spring council passed the business tax levy by-law at 0.5% of business assessment (By-laws 2248 in 2024, 2264 in 2025, 2277 in 2026). The city keeps a 5% administration fee and gives the rest to the Chamber of Commerce. Councillors said businesses support it; in 2026 the mayor praised the Chamber partnership.
status_detail: All three readings carried unanimously in each year; rate unchanged at 0.5%.
figures: Rate 0.5% unchanged (City Manager, 2024-04-16 0:48:47; 2025-05-06 0:10:03); Chamber of Commerce grant $225,000 in the 2025 financial plan (2025-03-04 package, "Some 2025 Programs").
reasons: businesses-support-it: Normally opposes a business tax, but businesses advocate keeping it. (Susan Penner); businesses-support-it: It empowers the Chamber to promote business. (Bill Hiebert)
public: No public comment recorded.
mover: Susan Penner (first reading each year); others rotate
notes: The Chamber has no written deliverables for this money on the public record. Chamber growth ranking is the mayor's statement, unverified.

title: Six-storey mixed-use building approved on Main Street
summary: Council unanimously approved a conditional use and height variance for a six-storey building at 362–366 Main Street with main-floor commercial (about half pre-leased, the applicant said) and 32 apartments. Every member called it the downtown density council had wanted for years; the mayor noted it took a developer to make it happen.
status_detail: CU-2024-04 (R24-116) and V-2024-04 (R24-117) approved unanimously.
figures: 6 storeys / 78 ft vs 5 storeys / 50 ft allowed (City Manager, transcript 0:24:12); 32 units (transcript 0:31:47).
reasons: market-decides: Downtown densification is developer-driven; council had to wait for a developer. (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: The applicant's representative (S.H., Avedo Inc.) said about half the commercial space was spoken for; one resident asked about unit count and parking. No objections.
notes: Applicant representative given by initials.

title: Other industrial-park cases: book-sale charity moved, caretaker homes refused
summary: Feb 2026: council let ROC Eastman move its approved occasional book sales (about 12 days a year) to a smaller unit at 110 Industrial Road, tied to that occupant. Sept 2026: council approved an industrial multi-use development at 75 Industrial Road but refused the owner's caretaker residence, saying industrial parks are not for homes. (In June 2024 a caretaker residence in a Park Road West industrial condo had been approved as an accessory use.)
status_detail: CU-2024-03 approved (R24-115); CU-2026-02 approved (R26-036); CU-2026-10 industrial use approved, caretaker residence denied (R26-181). All unanimous.
figures: ROC Eastman: 4 sales a year, about 12 days (applicant, transcript 2026-02-17 0:09:56).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Approving one caretaker home invites a stream of residences in the industrial park. (Susan Penner); fairness-precedent: Residences in heavy industrial zones do not fit the industry the city wants to attract. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Applicants: S.D. for ROC Eastman; J.L. for 75 Industrial Road (owner of Steinbach Fire Protection). No objectors.
mover: Damian Penner (R24-115); Jac Siemens (R26-036); Susan Penner (R26-181)
seconder: Bill Hiebert (R24-115); Michael Zwaagstra (R26-036); Jake Hiebert (R26-181)
notes: Applicants given by initials; businesses and charities named.

title: Business signs approved case by case (electronic signs, banners, fascia signs)
summary: Every business sign application in the period was approved: an electronic message sign for the Co-op on PTH 52 West (Nov 2024), illuminated fascia signs on Essex Drive (Jun 2025), sponsorship banners on Southeast Event Centre light poles (Sep 2025), and a larger electronic sign for Steinbach Credit Union on Main Street (Jul 2026). Councillor Zwaagstra said he could not recall council ever denying an electronic sign.
public: No objections recorded.
mover: Jac Siemens (R24-208, R25-172); Jake Hiebert (R25-114, R26-134); Damian Penner (R25-115)
seconder: Bill Hiebert (R24-208, R25-115); Michael Zwaagstra (R25-114, R26-134); Susan Penner (R25-172)
vote: unanimous (R25-115 vote not recorded in parsed minutes)
notes: Nov 5, 2024 and Jun 3, 2025 meetings have no transcripts; decisions from minutes.

title: Fleet services, towing yard, industrial multi-use and daycare approved
summary: Most business conditional uses were approved without debate: a daycare on Market Boulevard (Nov 2024), outdoor vehicle storage for a towing business on Keating Road and a three-unit industrial multi-use on Park Road West (May 2026), and a fleet-services business on the northern commercial corridor (Jul 2026), which members said fit well beside a truck dealer and card-lock, unlike the 2024 truck yard next to homes.
public: Owner representative A.K. (Schinkel Properties) welcomed another business; no objections.
mover: Susan Penner (R24-222); Michael Zwaagstra (R26-099); Jac Siemens (R26-100); Jake Hiebert (R26-148)
seconder: Damian Penner (R24-222); Bill Hiebert (R26-099); Jake Hiebert (R26-100); Jac Siemens (R26-148)
notes: May 19, 2026 meeting has no transcript; decisions from minutes.

title: New zoning by-law: less downtown parking, more uses as of right, shorter rules
summary: After a review begun in 2023, council directed changes (Dec 2024), gave the new Zoning By-law 2245 first and second reading (Apr 1, 2025) and third reading (Jan 20, 2026) after a Municipal Board hearing. Business-related changes: required parking in the central business district cut by one-third; residential allowed in mixed-use buildings downtown; offices, personal services, restaurants and clinics allowed as of right in the transitional overlay; main-floor commercial no longer pushed on multifamily; parking based on floor area; personal services made conditional in industrial zones; by-law shortened from 155 to 106 pages. The OCP (By-law 2244) added "planning for economic development".
status_detail: R24-234 (direction), R25-071/R25-072 (first/second reading, Zoning By-law), R25-069/070/184 (OCP), R25-181 (Municipal Board referral), R26-015 third reading — all unanimous. In force Jan 20, 2026.
figures: CBD parking reduced by 1/3 (Zwaagstra 2026-01-20 0:29:47); 155 to 106 pages (2025-04-01 2:00:15, medium-confidence speaker).
reasons: protect-residents: Some regulation is needed to protect land values and how people live and do business; not trying to be onerous. (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: Most public speakers on Apr 1, 2025 addressed emergency shelters becoming a conditional use, not business rules. Objections led to a Municipal Board hearing, which ordered no changes (City Manager, 2026-01-20 0:27:55).
mover: Susan Penner (R24-234, R25-071); Jac Siemens (R25-072); Michael Zwaagstra (R26-015)
seconder: Damian Penner (R24-234, R25-071); Jake Hiebert (R25-072, R26-015)
notes: Page counts from a medium-confidence speaker turn; not checked against the by-law documents.

title: Record permits and a "pro-growth, business-friendly" message
summary: Monthly building-permit reports became council's main public account of business growth: 2023 was a record commercial year (over $200 million in permits), 2024 had about $105 million including about $28 million commercial, and 2025 set a housing record. Members tied housing growth to labour supply for business. In April 2026 the mayor previewed his speech to the Manitoba Chamber of Commerce AGM, hosted in Steinbach for the first time: a diversified economy, low municipal taxes and a pro-growth council.
status_detail: Permit reports accepted monthly (routine). No city economic development strategy or targets replaced SED on the record.
figures: 2024: ~$105M total, $77M residential, ~$28M commercial (D. Penner, 2025-01-21 0:27:10); almost 120,000 sq ft commercial built in 2024 (Mayor, 0:28:12); 2023 over $200M, mostly commercial (Mayor, 2026-01-20 0:32:36); 365 dwelling units in 2025 (Mayor, 2026-01-20 0:31:51); population 20,011 in 2025, projected 36,936 by 2045; 28% immigrant workforce; total income about $844M (Mayor, 2026-04-21 0:00:36 and 0:04:50, unverified).
notes: Mayor's economic statistics (Apr 21, 2026) are his own and were not checked.

title: City objects to RM of Hanover zoning that legalized businesses on its northern edge
summary: The RM of Hanover approved a subdivision (summer 2024) and then proposed rezoning (By-law 2578-24) for land just north of the city on PTH 12 where non-agricultural businesses had already been built. Administration said this broke Hanover's own plan, provincial policy and the Steinbach–Hanover annexation agreement. Council filed a formal objection, saying businesses in Steinbach must meet city standards before building and fragmenting fringe land threatens future growth.
status_detail: R24-246 objection authorized unanimously. Outcome of Hanover's hearing not on the city record. In Sept 2026 council filed a similar objection to RM of La Broquerie plan/zoning changes in the transitional area (R26-192), mainly about rural residential density.
reasons: fairness-precedent: Steinbach holds developers to a standard (rezoning, traffic study, servicing) before permits; this land skipped those steps. (Jac Siemens); protect-residents: Fragmenting fringe land leaves nowhere for the city to grow. (Mayor Earl Funk)
notes: "Arm of Hanover" is the transcript's rendering of "RM of Hanover".

title: August Cove: 11 new city industrial lots after Acres Drive sold out
summary: The city applied, for its Steinbach Community Development Corporation (SCDC), to subdivide 11 new industrial lots on a new road, August Cove, south of Acres Drive, in a range of sizes including small lots for start-ups. The mayor said the 7 Acres Drive lots built in 2022 sold as soon as they were listed. Council later passed a plan of works for permanent drainage behind the lots. SCDC financial statements were accepted each year (2024, 2025, 2026).
status_detail: Subdivision approved (R25-012); Plan of Works By-law 2267 passed (R25-190, R25-213, R25-214); SCDC reports accepted (R24-138, R25-164, R26-170). All unanimous.
figures: 11 new lots (12 total), 0.68 to 2.5 acres plus one lot of almost 8 acres; Acres Drive (2022) created 7 lots (Mayor, transcript 0:10:11 and 0:10:47).
public: No objections (city was the applicant).
notes: No lot prices were stated in council. News (Feb 2026) reported the city had no industrial lots left; not stated in any transcript reviewed here.

title: Downtown farmers' market allowed at the Southeast Event Centre
summary: Council approved a weekly farmers' market in the Southeast Event Centre parking lot (Tuesdays, 2–6 p.m., June–September), calling it long overdue and an incubator for small businesses. A month earlier Councillor Damian Penner used his opening remarks to urge residents to buy local amid U.S. tariff threats.
status_detail: R25-053 carried unanimously.
figures: Tuesdays 2:00–6:00 p.m., June to end of September (R25-053).
public: Request came from Southeast Event Centre Group Inc.

title: Retail in the industrial park refused for a charity thrift store site (86 Industrial Rd)
summary: A developer sought retail use on a vacant, newly created industrial lot so that Adult & Teen Challenge could move its thrift store and counselling office off Main Street. Administration recommended denial: the land was sold at cost for industry and retail there would make the taxpayer subsidize commercial development and compete with private landlords. Because the approval would run with the whole title, council unanimously refused while praising the charity.
status_detail: CU-2025-01 denied (R25-034, unanimous).
figures: Charity needed about 10,000 sq ft; current Main St space about 7,000 sq ft (D.E., transcript 0:29:01, 0:31:00).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Subsidized industrial land used for retail makes the city a competitor of private commercial landlords. (Troy Warkentin, City Manager); fairness-precedent: Taxpayers build industrial parks and sell at or near cost to attract manufacturing jobs. (Jac Siemens); fairness-precedent: Protect the integrity of the industrial park; retail belongs in commercial zones; no precedent for whole-site retail. (Michael Zwaagstra); fairness-precedent: Whole-title approval could create a mini mall in the industrial park. (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: The applicant's representative (S.H., Avedo Inc.) and D.E. of Adult & Teen Challenge said no suitable commercial space existed and the Main Street building had to be vacated; they suggested condo or occupancy-based approval. No objectors.
notes: Applicant and charity representatives given by initials; organizations named.

title: Councillors ask to review or cap the Chamber's growing business-tax share
summary: At the 2025 financial plan hearing Councillor Susan Penner called the $225,000 Chamber grant "way out of line" (Winkler's chamber gets $65,000, she said) and asked for a study-session review. At first reading in 2025 she asked whether it should keep growing, be capped or partly redirected now the economic development pilot was ending; the mayor agreed it needed review. In 2026 Councillor Damian Penner and Susan Penner again said the growth may need a cap.
status_detail: No review result, cap or service agreement appears on the record; the 2026 levy passed unchanged at 0.5% with the full amount still going to the Chamber.
figures: Chamber grant $225,000 (S. Penner 2025-03-04 0:19:31; 2025 financial plan package); Winkler chamber $65,000 (S. Penner, unverified).
reasons: study-first: Agreed a review was needed at study session. (Mayor Earl Funk); businesses-support-it: Still working for now; community does not object. (Damian Penner)
public: None recorded.
notes: Study sessions are not recorded; whether the July 2025 review happened is unknown.

title: SED asks council to double its grant; immigration pilot questioned
summary: SED reported on its work, including the federal Rural Community Immigration Pilot (RCIP), which it joined without consulting the city and which carries no federal administration funding. SED had asked the city to double its public contribution. Councillors questioned the lack of consultation, transparency (SED would not say how many seats it had) and the risk of federal costs landing on the city. The written grant request was sent to a budget study session.
status_detail: Referred to an (unrecorded) study session on Mar 18, 2025; no increase appears on the record, and on Aug 5, 2025 council decided not to renew the grant at all (see 2025-sed-funding-ended).
figures: SED claim: direct economic impact over $12 million a year from workforce development (transcript 0:59:11, unverified). City share $65,000/yr (Siemens, Aug 5, 2025).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: Federal and provincial pilots without funding tend to become municipal costs. (Mayor Earl Funk); no-results: Asked whether the pilot drove the request to double city funding; no consultation before applying. (Michael Zwaagstra); study-first: Moved the grant request to study session. (Jac Siemens)
public: SED director M.B. said the pilot is an economic immigration pathway with no federal or provincial administration funding and that SED would seek more from both public and private sectors; an SED board member said reserves would carry the pilot. SED could not say which new businesses it had brought ("primarily lead generation"). SED's $12M impact figure is its own claim and unverified.
vote: not recorded (referred to study session by consensus)
decision_source: transcript; minutes say the request was "acknowledged"
notes: Budget study sessions are not recorded, so how council handled the doubling request before Aug 2025 is not on the record. Bill Hiebert's questions (label V) are low-confidence and not quoted.

title: Charity thrift store allowed in an existing industrial building, tied to the tenant
summary: Adult & Teen Challenge came back with an existing building at 16 Pioneer Road near MPI and Manitoba Hydro. Council approved retail sales there on condition the approval expires when the charity stops retail on the site, which members said limited the precedent.
status_detail: CU-2025-02 approved (R25-138, unanimous) with an expiry condition.
figures: Building about 23,000 sq ft (Zwaagstra, transcript 0:19:59).
public: M.F. and D.E. spoke for Adult & Teen Challenge / Association for Community Living; no objectors.
notes: Another councillor said "ordinarily I vote against any retail in industrial areas" (0:24:09) but the speaker is only medium-confidence (mapped to Damian Penner; wording resembles Jake Hiebert), so not quoted.

title: Kitchen-and-bath showroom refused in the industrial park, 5–1
summary: The Home Workshop Inc. sought retail sales (about 1,400 sq ft of display for cabinetry, fixtures, flooring and furniture) at 123 Industrial Road, with manufacturing staying in Mitchell. Councillor Siemens moved to approve with conditions; the motion died for lack of a seconder. Council then denied it 5–1.
status_detail: CU-2025-03 denied (R25-144), Siemens against; Susan Penner excused.
figures: About 1,400 sq ft retail display; three rear rental bays (minutes 7.2).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Industrial lots were created and sold at cost to support manufacturing; retail is only a conditional use (minutes 7.4). (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: Resident G.S. asked whether industrial lots are subsidized and whether cheaper land draws retail away from commercial zones (minutes 7.3).
notes: No transcript of the Jul 15, 2025 meeting is in the collection; everything here is from the minutes. Applicant representative (A.G.) given by initials; business named.

title: Council ends the economic development office grant after 2025
summary: Council had matched private funding for an economic development office ($65,000 a year, 2021–2025) with a sunset of Dec 31, 2025. Councillor Siemens moved not to renew, saying the hoped-for development had not come; both Hieberts said the results were not there. The mayor said economic development is a partnership and one office was never going to do it alone. No replacement was set up.
status_detail: R25-158: the city "does not renew its grant funding commitment upon the conclusion of the current term effective December 31, 2025". No city economic development office or agreement replaced it on the record through Nov 2026.
figures: $65,000 a year from the city, 2021–2025 (Siemens, transcript 0:24:52).
reasons: no-results: Has not seen the development hoped for; office struggled to find its footing and changed vision and staff. (Jac Siemens); no-results: Measured by results (contacts, interest, relocations) and saw none; $65,000 would be futile (speaker map low; news attribution). (Jake Hiebert); no-results: Did not see the value expected; duplication with the Chamber (speaker map low; news attribution). (Bill Hiebert); partner-money: If continued, an office should run under the Chamber using the funding the city already gives the Chamber. (Jac Siemens); not-council-role: Council's role is creating an environment; landowners, developers, the Chamber and the CDC do attraction as a team. (Mayor Earl Funk); market-decides: Landowners and business owners are the community's unofficial economic development officers. (Jac Siemens)
public: No public speakers. (News coverage reported the Chamber accepted that business-attraction expectations were not fully met and that SED planned to continue regionally on reserves; not verified here.)
vote: unanimous (Susan Penner and Damian Penner excused, R25-153)
notes: The two Hiebert speakers are low-confidence in the speaker map; quotes are marked medium only because news coverage matches the same words to the same councillors (that article was not re-checked here).

title: Cannabis retail plebiscite request from TobaGrown refused 6–1
summary: TobaGrown wrote asking council to hold a plebiscite on allowing cannabis retail sales alongside the Oct 28, 2026 municipal election. Council resolved not to initiate such a plebiscite by resolution. Councillor Siemens voted against the refusal.
status_detail: R25-167 carried 6–1. No cannabis question appeared on the 2026 ballot by council resolution.
public: Correspondence and request from TobaGrown (business) acknowledged (minutes item 14). No reasons are recorded in the minutes.
notes: The Aug 19, 2025 meeting has no transcript in the collection, so council's stated reasons could not be checked. Under Manitoba law a plebiscite could also be triggered by petition (not verified here).

title: Gas station's request to halve street landscaping refused
summary: Suncor Energy sought a 50% cut in required street-edge landscaping at North Gate Drive. Nobody attended for the applicant; council denied it unanimously, citing the city's aesthetics.
status_detail: V-2025-24 denied (R25-178, unanimous).
figures: 50% reduction requested (minutes).
reasons: protect-residents: Landscaping rules exist for the city's overall aesthetics; no applicant attended to explain. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: No one attended.

title: Mayor's lunches with business owners and advocacy for local firms
summary: Speaking on the 2026 business tax, Mayor Funk described regular mayor's lunches with local business people (with a Councillor Penner) and said council had advocated federally for some local businesses, working with the Chamber.
status_detail: Described as ongoing; no list of meetings or advocacy outcomes is on the public record.
notes: Which Councillor Penner attends is not stated.

title: RBC ramp on Main Street right-of-way approved like seasonal patios
summary: RBC asked to put an emergency accessible ramp on the public right-of-way at its Main Street branch. Administration treated it like the seasonal permits council grants for Main Street patios (three operating) and recommended an annual permit; council approved.
status_detail: R26-189 approved unanimously, subject to annual review and permit.
figures: 3 Main Street patios operating under seasonal permits (City Manager, transcript 1:17:33).
